newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norwegian business wants premier to stay--report.
newsitem.headline: Norwegian business wants premier to stay--report.

text.p: Norwegian corporate leaders hope that Prime Minister Thorbjoern Jagland's ruling Labour Party will retain power in the elections in September, an opinion poll released at the weekend said.

The Feedback Research survey, commissioned by financial daily Dagens Naeringsliv, said 47 percent of executives in 208 companies polled wanted Jagland to lead Norway in the next four-year legislature.
His top challengers received 16 percent each in the poll.
"This confirms that industry favours the Labour Party," election analyst Bernt Aardal told Dagens Naeringsliv.
The Labour Party has been in power since 1990 and generally represents stability to financial markets.
The crown has weakened considerably recently partly because of growing market concern that the Labour government might lose the September 15 election, according to financial analysts.
Markets are worried that a centrist government would lead to a loosening of fiscal policy. The crown fell to 4.2015 against the German mark at 1400 GMT on Friday from 4.1950 on Thursday.

The survey said only 16 percent of Norwegian business leaders preferred either Kjell Magne Bondevik, prime minister candidate for the Christian People's Party, or Johan J. Jakobsen, the Centre Party's candidate for the job.
Aardal said the poll was a vote of confidence for the Labour Party and that Jagland, who succeeded veteran premier Gro Harlem Brundtland last October, was not necessarily popular himself.
Jagland's support for continued state ownership of the country's two largest banks has won him few friends in the markets.
As many as 29 percent of the executives wanted neither Jagland nor Bondevik or Jakobsen as prime minister and eight percent were undecided, the poll said.

The three centrist parties -- the Christian People's Party, the Centre Party and liberal Venstre -- have said they will increase public spending if they gain enough votes to form a coalition government.

They want to invest more of Norway's oil wealth in schools and public transportation while the Labour government is setting aside the budget surplus -- projected at 57.3 billion crowns this year -- in the State Petroleum Fund for investment in overseas securities.
The Labour Party, which won 36.9 percent of the votes in the 1993 election, received 30.6 percent of voter support in a monthly opinion poll published by daily Aftenposten a week ago.
It put the total for the three centrist parties at 28.8 percent.

"It is no longer a political dream to imagine Johan J. Jakobsen or Kjell Magne Bondevik being given the chance to form a government in the next legislature," Aftenposten said on a comment on Saturday.
"An election outcome where the centrist parties as a group becomes as big as the Labour Party cannot be ruled out."
The Labour Party is by far the biggest among the eight parties represented in the 165-seat Storting, or parliament.
